Directional splitting and holomorphic compatibility

Written and self-checked by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra, October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

Suppose several closed sets of covector directions cover all directions. A hyperfunction can be separated into pieces whose singular directions lie in those sets, without introducing a new singular direction. The pieces are not unique. Their exact ambiguity consists of antisymmetric exchanges on pairwise intersections. When the directional sets are convex, these exchanges become holomorphic functions on sums of imaginary approach cones. This gives a concrete description of which collections of holomorphic sides represent the same hyperfunction.

The proof uses the complete carrier topology and spherical recovery in Holomorphic boundary values without growth bounds, Proposition 2; its Theorems 3–7 supply analytic wavefronts, boundary values, uniqueness and the converse wedge representation. The bounded quotient and closure-supported extension are proved in Hyperfunctions from local analytic sources, in the sections on bounded domains, compact sections and extension. The earlier distribution arguments in Holomorphic decompositions of tempered distributions, Theorem 5, and Boundary regularity and conic decomposition, Theorems 4–5, explain the angular geometry and algebra. Here their limits are taken in analytic-functional carrier seminorms; no finite distributional order or polynomial boundary bound is assumed. Finite-measure integration, compactness and continuous limits use the supplied integration foundation, Sections 15–16 and metric foundation, Sections 12–13.

The exact relation among holomorphic sides

Fix a finite cover of by closed convex pointed cones . Let . Empty directional cones cause no difficulty: gives .

For an open convex cone , write for the vector space of holomorphic germs at from , in the precise local wedge sense of Theorem 4 of the preceding lesson. A representative is holomorphic on an open set containing all sufficiently short imaginary displacements in each closed subcone, locally uniformly over compact real subsets. Two representatives are equal when they agree on such smaller wedges. Let mean ordinary holomorphic germs on a complex neighborhood of ; their restrictions are real analytic functions. Use ordinary trace as their boundary map.

These conventions cover cone sums that contain zero. For the other cones use the growth-free boundary map. Its cone independence, uniqueness and linearity make well defined. The finite direct sum is simply a finite tuple.

This is an equality of the described vector spaces, with no topology on the quotient being asserted.

Two choices of cone cover give the same intrinsic hyperfunction space through (H3). One can compare them using their combined finite cover: insert zero components for the additional cones and apply the proved kernel description. No assertion that individual angular pieces are canonical is involved.

Exercises with full solutions

Exercise 1 (basic) — a finite angular atom. Let and be as in Lemma 1, and let with . Give the interior wavefront bound and explain why it need not be an equality.

Solution. Formula (A3) permits only covectors , , and only where fails to extend at . If , the functional is integration of on , whose restriction to is the analytic constant . It has no interior analytic wavefront, even for . The boundary term in (A3) is not an interior singularity.

Exercise 2 (basic) — two disjoint directional sets. In dimension one take , . Show that two subordinate decompositions of the same hyperfunction differ by transferring a real analytic function between the two pieces.

Solution. Their cone intersection is empty in the punctured line. Theorem 2 gives with empty wavefront. The projection theorem makes real analytic. Thus and . Conversely every such transfer preserves both directional bounds, since adding an analytic function does not enlarge wavefront. On the holomorphic side the approach cones are the positive and negative half-lines, whose sum is all of ; their exchange is therefore a holomorphic germ across the real base.

Exercise 6 (advanced) — a genuine three-way cancellation. For three cones as in Theorem 4, choose germs on the respective sum cones. Form a tuple whose total boundary is zero, and verify the signs without imposing a common domain on all three germs.

Solution. On the individual approach cones set Each restriction is defined by Lemma 3. For each pair, (H4) identifies its two boundary values on , so the opposite signs cancel. Only the finitely many germs entering one component must be restricted to a common smaller -wedge; their intersection still has the required local heights. There is no need to evaluate all three pair germs on one common complex domain.

Exercise 7 (advanced) — an angular piece of a zero class. Let , , , and . Show that , but both individual angular restrictions are nonzero analytic functions.

Solution. The compact functional is carried at a boundary point of , so its quotient class is zero. The two one-point angular pieces are, on , Indeed the off-carrier domain of contains both displaced copies of every compact subinterval of ; local restriction of the angular functional therefore equals its ordinary analytic trace, as in the last part of Lemma 1. Neither function is identically zero. If, for example, vanished for every , the one-variable identity principle would make vanish on its connected continuation domain This domain is connected: shrink the imaginary coordinate to zero and then move on the real axis. But the defining spherical integral has , and this positive integral is finite. The other sign is identical. Spherical recovery gives on . Thus the two pieces cancel but do not individually vanish. This explicitly disproves descent of these particular angular maps through the boundary quotient.

Exercise 8 (advanced) — an essential singularity split into two sides. For on a real interval containing zero, let Describe a directional splitting, prove that at least one piece is not a distribution, and determine the ambiguity among all splittings with the same two half-line bounds.

Solution. Take and . The positive-dual bound puts their wavefronts in the positive and negative covector rays, respectively. Off zero both sides have the ordinary analytic trace, so the only possible singular base point is zero. The preceding lesson, Exercises 2 and 8, proves that the upper boundary and the full jump are not distributions, using the super-polynomial value and the infinite nonzero point moments, respectively. In particular the exhibited upper piece is not a distribution. Also no decomposition of can have both pieces distributions, since their sum would be a distribution. Exercise 2 shows that every other subordinate splitting differs by an analytic transfer ; the analytic functions are distributions, so each piece's distributional or nondistributional character is preserved by this ambiguity. This calculation requires no polynomial growth estimate for defining either boundary.

Programme proofs and mathematical source

The carrier and hyperfunction arguments used here are fully available in Analytic tests and real carriers, Localizing analytic sources without analytic cutoffs, Hyperfunctions from local analytic sources, and Holomorphic boundary values without growth bounds. The first two are the proved foundations of the last two; the particular interfaces used above are identified at their points of use.

  • Lars Hörmander, The Analysis of Linear Partial Differential Operators I: Distribution Theory and Fourier Analysis, reprint of the second edition, Springer, 2003, doi:10.1007/978-3-642-61497-2, Section 9.3, Lemma 9.3.6, Theorem 9.3.7 and the ensuing interpretation by holomorphic sides. These supply the mathematical angular and conic decomposition results and Martineau compatibility relation. The carrier-limit proof, explicit representative correction, convex geometry, organization, examples, exercises and figure here are independently expressed.

General analytic pullback and the further tensor, product, integration and kernel operations require their own proofs. They are not conclusions of this lesson.
